title: Healing Promised to a Ruined City
overview: While Babylon's army is breaking Jerusalem apart, God promises through Jeremiah that the city will be healed, forgiven, filled with joy again, and ruled by a just king from David's family.

parts.label: An invitation to ask (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Jeremiah is still held under guard while Babylon besieges Jerusalem, and God, introduced as the maker of the earth, invites him to call out and promises to show him things beyond his reach. Those things are most likely the city's coming restoration, which seemed impossible at the time.

parts.label: Ruin now, healing later (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Houses and even royal palaces were torn down to shore up the defenses against the enemy's earth ramps, and the text bluntly says they would fill with the dead as God's anger at the city's wrongdoing. Then comes a sharp turn: God promises to heal the city, bring both Judah and Israel home, wipe away their guilt, and make the city something other nations marvel at.

parts.label: The sounds of life return (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Jeremiah had earlier warned that the sounds of weddings would go silent, and here they come back, along with worshippers singing a thanksgiving line also found in Psalm 136. Shepherds counting their sheep one by one as they pass under the hand pictures a calm, lived-in countryside where none are lost.

parts.label: A just king from David (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: This repeats an earlier promise from Jeremiah 23 of a new "Branch," a king from David's family who will rule fairly, and here Jerusalem itself receives a name saying the LORD is the source of its rightness and rescue. Many scholars think the name contrasts with the current king Zedekiah, whose own name means something like "the LORD is righteous" but who did not live up to it.

parts.label: As sure as day and night (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: God ties the lasting line of David's kings and of the priests from the tribe of Levi to the steady cycle of day and night, saying one can no more fail than the other. No king from David's line actually ruled after Babylon, so Jewish readers have looked to a future anointed king and Christians read the promise as met in Jesus, while scholars note this closing section is missing from the ancient Greek translation.

parts.label: Not rejected after all (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: Some were saying God had thrown away the two groups he once chose, probably meaning the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and were treating the people as finished. God answers with the same image of day and night: as long as those hold, he will not abandon Jacob's descendants or David's line, but will restore them with compassion.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises of an unbroken royal line and priesthood are fulfilled spiritually in Jesus and the church, or still point to a future, literal restoration of the nation of Israel.
think: When something in your life or the world looks past repair, what would make a promise of restoration believable to you, and what would make it ring hollow?
